title: The river bank
hook: a tree on the riverbank can fall at any time, says the Oankar

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the pandit reads: cartloads of books, and only one thing counted. Your line was read and understand. Which line did you keep long enough to change something? Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

There's a tree at the edge of a river. Its leaves are full, its shade is good, birds sit in it. From the path it looks like it will stand forever. But down at the waterline, where nobody looks, the current is working. A little soil goes every day. Then one ordinary afternoon, no storm, no warning, the bank lets go and the tree leans into the water. The Oankar, Guru Nanak's poem on the letters, stops on that picture: a tree on the riverbank can fall at any time. Today: the river bank.
screen: `A TREE AT THE WATER'S EDGE.` → `THE CURRENT WORKS UNSEEN.` → `ONE DAY THE BANK LETS GO.`

segments.voice: Where we are: the Oankar walks through the letters, and at each one it sets down a teaching. Here, the teaching is a picture. A tree standing on a riverbank, which can fall at any time. Notice what the picture does not say. It doesn't say the tree is weak, or foolish, or doing anything wrong. A tree on a riverbank is just where it is. The danger isn't in the tree. It's in the ground under it, which is slowly being carried away. That's one way the Guru Granth Sahib speaks of a human life. Not as a disaster waiting to happen, but as something standing on ground that is always moving. The same picture shows up in the verses of Sheikh Farid, the Sufi poet whose words are also kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: a tree on the riverbank, how long can it keep its footing? How long can water stay in a pot of unbaked clay? Two voices, two different worlds, one image, kept side by side in the same scripture. So what is the picture for? Not fear. In the Oankar, the shortness of life turns into a question of timing. If the bank can give way any day, then the things that matter can't wait for a safer season. The Name, the apology, the visit, the kindness you meant to get to: now is the bank you're standing on. In Sikh teaching, that's clarity, not gloom. The current is real. So is the shade, while it lasts.
screen: `A TREE THAT CAN FALL AT ANY TIME.` · `THE DANGER IS IN THE GROUND.` · `SHEIKH FARID: HOW LONG ITS FOOTING?` · `NOT FEAR: A QUESTION OF TIMING.` · then, large: `THE BANK GIVES WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by water. If there's a river, a pond, a fountain or the sea near you, go and stand at its edge. If not, stand by a running tap, or stand where you are and picture a riverbank under you. This time, let the attention go to your feet, not the water. Feel the ground taking your weight. It's holding today. Stay with that for a few breaths: the water moving, the ground holding, for now. Then let one thing come to mind that you've been putting off for a safer season. Just name it. If you pray, you can remember the One beside the water. If you don't, simply let the water keep time. The bell holds the time.
The river bank. In the Oankar, a tree on the riverbank can fall at any time: life stands on moving ground, so what matters can't wait. Today's word.
Your line: the bank gives way. Today, do the one thing you named by the water, or take the first small step toward it, before evening. Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Sikh hymns recall how short life is, as a reason to remember the Name now; the verses of Sheikh Farid, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, are sung and read with the Gurus' hymns.

options: despair: nothing lasts, so nothing matters.
ignore it: the leaves look fine.

original.note: kandhi: the riverbank, as in Sheikh Farid's salok of the tree on the bank.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy picture about death.
what it means: life stands on moving ground, so the things that matter belong to today.
what a scholar hears: the image is shared by the Oankar and Sheikh Farid's saloks, two voices kept side by side in one scripture.

sources.ref: Salok Sheikh Farid ('kandhee utai rukhrraa'), Ang 1382
